newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank keeping loose money policy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank keeping loose money policy.

text.p: Taiwan's central banker said on Tuesday the bank would maintain its stable-to-loose monetary policy and not lower its money-supply growth targets, citing expectations of economic recovery and growing liquidity demand in 1997.
"The economy will gradually recover next year and demand for liquidity will increase," bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong told reporters at a year-end news conference.
"The priority is to maintain the stability of consumer prices and finance. We will continue in future to execute our stable-to-loose monetary policy," Sheu said.

Sheu said the bank's target for growth of the broadest measure of money supply, M2, would not be lowered from its 9-14 percent level despite a top state economic planner's assertion that a reduction to 8-13 percent had been agreed.
"The main reason that M2 growth did not meet the target zone was that the economic recovery has not been as fast as projected and (therefore) demand for liquidity was weak," Sheu said.

The central bank and other agencies have said a modest recovery begun in the fourth quarter of 1996 would pick up steam in 1997. The central bank, in a package of year-end predictions, said gross domestic product would grow 6.17 percent in 1997, up from its own full-year 1996 forecast of 5.66.

Sheu did not stray from central bank's position, stated repeatedly in recent months, that monetary policy should be kept where it is to ensure adequate financing for any recovery without fuelling inflation or undermining citizens' deposits.

Sheu said the central bank's policy in principle was to gradually reduce bank's reserve requirements so as to ensure adequate liquidity in the market, but made clear that it had no plans to do so now.
The bank has reduced banks' reserve requirements five times since mid-1995 and the lack of a significant impact on Taiwan's hoped-for recovery has sobered Sheu about their effectiveness.
Sheu has said often that reserve requirement adjustments were no cure-all for an ailing economy.
As for Taiwan's currency, Sheu said the central bank's policy was to allow market forces to determine the rate of the Taiwan dollar against foreign currencies.
The central bank, hoping to bolster exports, inspired a modest depreciatation in May 1996 by saying it no longer would defend the rate at T$27.5 to the U.S. dollar.
But the rate rebounded by July and has held firm at the decade-old defence level ever since with almost no volatility.
